notes.h: Background: anglicisation and the national mood of the early 1880s
notes.b: By the early 1880s many Irish people felt that their own language, games and customs were being pushed aside by English ones, just as politics was stirring strong national feeling. The GAA grew out of both worries.
points: The Famine and the heavy emigration that followed weakened rural Irish society and the Irish language, so English language and customs spread, especially in towns and schools.

Anglicisation means the replacement of Irish language, dress, games and customs by English ones. De-anglicisation is the effort to reverse this by reviving Irish language, games and customs, and the GAA was an early example.
The Gaelic Union (1880), successor to the Society for the Preservation of the Irish Language (1876), was formed to preserve Irish, so the language already had a society while games had none.

The Land War began in 1879, when Michael Davitt founded the Land League with Parnell as president to defend tenant farmers against landlords. From 1880 the Irish Party (Home Rule Party), led by Parnell, sought self-government for Ireland.

A Fenian revival was also under way. The IRB (Irish Republican Brotherhood, the Fenians) was a secret, oath-bound society that wanted an Irish republic won by force, so it looked for new organisations to join.

The Catholic Church was a powerful influence on nationalist Ireland and was generally constitutional, preferring peaceful politics to secret societies. This is why the Church and the IRB later came into conflict inside the GAA.
Irish Ireland was the later cultural-nationalist idea of building the nation on native language, games and traditions. It was developed after 1891, but the GAA is one of its roots.
notes.tip: Define anglicisation and de-anglicisation in a sentence each and tie the GAA to them. Essays on the GAA are expected to link it to both ideas.

notes.b: Before the GAA, organised sport in Ireland followed English rules and belonged mainly to the gentry and middle class, while the native game of hurling had declined. That gap is what the GAA set out to fill.
points: Organised athletics followed English-style amateur rules that excluded “mechanics, artisans and labourers” (people who earned a living by manual work), so most working people and most farmers could not compete as amateurs.

Rugby, cricket and later soccer were played in schools, in garrison towns (towns with an army barracks) and among the gentry. The Irish Rugby Football Union was formed in 1879 and the Irish Football Association (soccer, Belfast-based) in 1880.
Hurling had declined since the Famine, as landlord patronage ended and rural communities shrank. It survived in parts of Galway and Munster, including Tipperary, Limerick, Cork and Clare.
Hurling was played under varying local rules, and football had no national code, so teams from different districts could not easily play one another on agreed terms.
Michael Cusack founded the Metropolitan Hurling Club in Dublin in 1882 and pushed for standard rules, which shows that the idea of a national code existed before the GAA.
notes.tip: Contrast the exclusive English-style amateur athletics with the GAA’s promise to open sport to all classes. That contrast is the heart of the background.

notes.h: The founders: Michael Cusack and Maurice Davin
notes.b: Two very different men started the GAA. Cusack supplied the drive and the ideas, and Davin supplied the respect that made others join.
points: Michael Cusack was born at Carron, Co. Clare, in 1847 and died in 1906. He was a teacher who ran a Dublin academy preparing pupils for exams.
Cusack was forceful and quarrelsome, which made him a tireless promoter but a difficult colleague, a point that matters when he falls out with fellow officers in 1886.
Cusack’s fame outlived him in literature: he was the model for “the Citizen”, a character in James Joyce’s novel Ulysses.
Maurice Davin was born in 1842 near Carrick-on-Suir, Co. Tipperary, and died in 1927. He was a champion athlete in weight-throwing and a champion rower.
Davin was respected for his fairness, so he was the natural first president of the GAA (1884–1889). His standing gave the new body credibility with athletes and clubs.
Do not mix the two up: Cusack was the Clare-born founder, agitator and secretary, removed in 1886, while Davin was the Tipperary sportsman and president, who resigned in 1889.
notes.tip: Examiners and source questions reward knowing each man’s role. Cusack was the founder and a secretary; Davin was the first president.

notes.b: In the autumn of 1884 Cusack went from writing about Irish athletics to calling a meeting, and the GAA was founded at Thurles within weeks.
points: In October 1884 (on 11 October) Cusack’s article “A Word About Irish Athletics” appeared in United Ireland, calling for a national body to revive native athletics.
United Ireland was Parnell’s nationalist weekly, edited by William O’Brien, so the call reached exactly the nationalist readers Cusack wanted.
Cusack and Davin then sent out invitations to a meeting at Hayes’ Hotel, Thurles, Co. Tipperary.
The meeting took place on Saturday 1 November 1884. Seven men attended, among them Cusack, Davin and John Wyse Power, a journalist.
Davin was elected president and Cusack was elected one of the secretaries.
The aims were to revive Irish games, to open athletics to all classes, and to promote physical fitness and national pride.
The full title was the Gaelic Athletic Association for the Preservation and Cultivation of National Pastimes, where “pastimes” means games and sports.
notes.tip: Keep the three 1884 dates apart: Cusack’s article in October, the Hayes’ Hotel meeting on 1 November, and Croke’s letter in December. A bare “founded in Thurles” earns little; give who, where and when.

notes.h: The patrons and Archbishop Croke’s letter
notes.b: Cusack won the backing of the most powerful figures in nationalist Ireland. Their names gave the GAA respectability and publicity it could not have won alone.
points: Thomas Croke, Archbishop of Cashel from 1875, had supported the tenants in the Land War and was a known nationalist, so his name carried weight with farmers.
In a letter of December 1884 Croke agreed to become patron. He condemned the imitation of English games and manners and urged the revival of Irish pastimes as an act of national self-respect.
Parnell and Davitt both agreed to be patrons (1884–85), which linked the GAA to the Home Rule movement and to the land movement.
Davitt saw the GAA as a way of drawing working people and farmers into the national movement, and as a way of reviving Irish games to break from English influence. He wrote and spoke in support.
William O’Brien, editor of United Ireland, promised the GAA regular space in the paper, which gave it free publicity.
Croke’s letter was widely printed and made the GAA respectable, and many priests became club presidents and organisers.
notes.tip: In source questions, say who is writing and why. Croke writes as a churchman and nationalist with a purpose, and Parnell, Davitt and O’Brien are supporters, so none of them is a neutral witness.

notes.b: The GAA set rules that separated Irish sport from English sport and built a structure on the parish. These choices explain both its quick growth and some of its later quarrels.
points: The first rules for hurling and Gaelic football were drawn up chiefly by Davin in 1885, replacing the old local variations with national codes.
Competition was open to all classes, so the English amateur definition that excluded manual workers was rejected.
The GAA was itself amateur (players were not paid), and it set out to keep money and professionalism out of sport.
The foreign games ban stopped members from playing foreign games such as rugby, soccer, cricket and hockey. Its purpose was de-anglicisation, and the early ban concerned playing, not attending.

Members of the Royal Irish Constabulary (the police force) and the British armed forces were also barred, because they represented British rule. The first ban covers games and the second covers people.
Each club was based on a parish, with county committees and a Central Council above them, and an annual convention (the yearly delegate meeting) that was usually held in Thurles.
The parish structure matched the Catholic Church’s own organisation, which made it easy for priests to take part.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the foreign games ban, which is about games, with the bar on RIC and military members, which is about people.

notes.b: The parish club system let the GAA spread very fast, and in 1887 it launched its first All-Ireland championships.
points: The GAA spread first in the south and west and then to the midlands and beyond. Within a few years hundreds of clubs had affiliated (joined the Association).
Matches became local occasions, with large crowds, bands and parades of club men. The crowds also brought problems, such as drinking.
The first All-Ireland championship was held in 1887 with an open draw and no provincial stage. It was decided in 1888, so its finals were played in 1888, not 1887.
The first hurling final was played at Birr (then King’s County, now Co. Offaly) on 1 April 1888. Thurles, representing Tipperary, beat Meelick, representing Galway.
The first football final was played in April 1888. Commercials, representing Limerick, beat Young Irelands (Dundalk), representing Louth.
Cusack founded a weekly paper, The Celtic Times, in 1887 to promote Gaelic games.
notes.tip: Say the 1887 championship was decided in April 1888. Do not give scores for the finals.

notes.h: The IRB, the clerical reaction and the crisis (1886–1889)
notes.b: The GAA’s success made it a target for the Fenians and a worry for the Church, and its own leaders fell out. These are the first of the difficulties examiners ask about.
points: Members of the IRB joined in large numbers, using clubs and county boards (the committees of each county) to recruit and to gain influence. Widespread local clubs gave them a ready network.
Dublin Castle (the seat of British government in Ireland) watched the GAA closely, and RIC reports described it as a front for Fenianism.
Cusack was removed as secretary in 1886 after quarrelling with fellow officers. The causes are disputed, so the safe statement is the date and the quarrels.
At the Thurles convention of 1887, IRB-linked and moderate delegates contested control of the Central Council.

Archbishop Croke and other bishops grew uneasy, and the Church was concerned about drink and discipline. Croke wrote to a GAA convention complaining of drinking at games, and in some places priests withdrew from clubs.
Davin resigned as president in 1889 amid the disputes and divisions of those years.
The IRB’s hold on the Central Council was strong by the later 1880s, and the stronger it grew, the more the Church held back.
notes.tip: Keep the dates apart: Cusack was removed in 1886 and Davin resigned in 1889. Do not give the IRB as the proven cause of either.

notes.h: The American tour and the Parnell split (1888–1891)
notes.b: Two blows in quick succession, an expensive overseas tour and the split in Irish nationalism, brought the association close to collapse.
points: In autumn 1888 about fifty hurlers and athletes, known as the American Invasion, toured the United States, with Irish-American support in cities such as New York and Boston.
The tour lost money and left debts. It also disrupted the 1888 championship, which was left unfinished and played off in 1889, and some of the athletes stayed in America.
The O’Shea divorce case (November 1890) damaged Parnell, and the Irish Party split in December 1890 (in Committee Room 15) into pro- and anti-Parnell groups.
The split divided GAA members, with the IRB generally favouring Parnell and Church-minded members opposing him. This is the same man who had been a GAA patron in 1884 but now caused division.
Parnell died on 6 October 1891, which left the association demoralised.
By 1891 membership and the number of clubs had collapsed, and a few county boards were all that remained in many areas.
The GAA recovered slowly in the 1890s, with a new generation of leaders and the support of the Gaelic revival (the renewed interest in Irish language and culture).
notes.tip: Do not confuse the 1888 American tour, an athletes’ trip, with the 1888 championship, which it left unfinished. In essays, pair the tour’s debts with the Parnell split.

notes.h: Why the GAA survived and how it dealt with its difficulties
notes.b: The main exam question on this case study asks how the GAA dealt with its difficulties to 1891. The answers are its organisation, its patrons, the appeal of the games and a willingness to change leaders.
points: The parish-based club system meant that local clubs could carry on even when the Central Council quarrelled.
The patronage of Croke and the clergy gave the association moral authority, and priests helped to restore order in clubs.
The appeal of hurling and football, and of local rivalry, was strong in itself and did not depend on politics.
The removal of Cusack and the departure of Davin showed an attempt to settle disputes by changing leaders rather than breaking up the body.
Links with the nationalist movement, through Parnell, Davitt and the IRB, gave the GAA energy but also exposed it to the Parnell split.
Its identity as an Irish-only, amateur body made it a symbol of de-anglicisation, which the later Irish Ireland ideas built on.
notes.tip: For the 40-mark question, open with a thesis, then give three or four difficulties, each paired with how it was handled and dated. Choose from IRB infiltration and Dublin Castle suspicion, Church unease, quarrels among leaders, the American tour and debt, and the Parnell split.

notes.h: Documents and the views of each side
notes.b: Documents on the early GAA are letters, speeches and reports. Each was written by someone with a purpose, so judging a source means asking who wrote it, when, why and for whom.
points: Cusack’s article of October 1884 and his invitations are founding documents, expressing the aim of opening athletics to all classes. He was the founder, so he is not neutral.
Croke’s letter of December 1884 is the best-known statement of the GAA’s national purpose, and it should be read as a clerical and nationalist appeal against English fashions.
Croke’s later complaint to a convention about drinking at games shows a churchman’s concern about discipline, and a favourable picture of crowds and bands can be set against it.
Davitt’s letters and speeches show the GAA’s links with the land movement, and Parnell’s patronage brought political prestige.
Unionist newspapers and Dublin Castle reports describe the GAA as seditious or as a cover for the IRB. They were hostile, so they may exaggerate.
Reports of conventions and county board meetings are evidence of the dispute between moderates and the IRB, though they are written by partisans (people taking a side).

Marcus de Búrca, The GAA: A History (1980), is a full institutional history. W.F. Mandle, The Gaelic Athletic Association and Irish Nationalist Politics, 1884–1924 (1987), stresses the political and IRB links, and Paul Rouse, Sport and Ireland: A History (2015), is a later study.
notes.tip: Name the author’s role and purpose, and say what a source shows and what it cannot show. When comparing documents from different dates, quote the wording and link it to the wider picture, such as crowds and discipline against drink and weak local clubs.

notes.b: The GAA’s early years show both a cultural achievement and the cost of political entanglement. A good answer gives both sides and a judgement.
points: Achievement: it created a national mass organisation open to all classes, standardised the rules of hurling and football and built a parish network.
Limit: IRB entanglement, the quarrel with the Church, debts from the American tour and the Parnell split brought it close to collapse by 1891.
Contemporary nationalists saw it as a school for national feeling, while unionists and the authorities saw it as Fenian, and bishops saw it as useful but dangerous.
Later historians see the GAA as a central part of the cultural nationalism of the 1880s, which anticipated the Gaelic League (1893, founded by Douglas Hyde and Eoin MacNeill) and Irish Ireland.
notes.tip: Examiners want both columns, achievements and quarrels, with the IRB and the Church as the central controversies, and a judgement between national identity and entanglement in politics.

keyTerms.definition: The process by which English language, dress, games and customs replaced Irish ones, which the GAA and later the Gaelic League opposed.
The effort to reverse anglicisation by reviving the Irish language, games and customs; Hyde used the word in 1892.
The cultural nationalist idea that the nation should be built on Irish language, games and Catholic identity, rather than English models.
The body founded at Thurles on 1 November 1884 to promote Irish games and athletics.
The GAA rule banning members from playing or attending games such as cricket, rugby and soccer.
A GAA club based on a parish, the local unit of the association.
The GAA’s governing body, whose control was contested between moderates and the IRB in the later 1880s.
The 1888 tour of the United States by Irish hurlers and athletes, which lost money and disrupted the association.
The principle that sportsmen play without payment; the GAA kept it but opened sport to all classes.
